Abul Hashem ------ Petitioner
Vs.

full_judgment: 5. Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the preemptee opposite parties on the other hand submits that sufficiency or insufficiency of the evidence is a matter to be looked into by the court of facts and in the instant case both the courts below on due consideration of the evidence and materials on record arrived at a concurrent finding of fact that the deed in question is not a deed of sale but a deed of release. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant case there is no necessity of examining any attesting witness or the scribe of the deed in question in support of their case by the pre-emptee opposite parties inasmuch as attesting witnesses only prove the execution of the documents and they are not competent to prove the contents of the same and in the instant case the positive case of the pre-emptee opposite parties is that the pre-emptor in collusion with the executants of the deeds managed to write the deed as a deed of sale instead of ''Nadabi'' deed. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no bar in relying on the single testimony of a witness if it appears to be true to the Court and in the instant case both the courts below relying on the testimony of DW 3 arrived at a finding that no consideration was passed in respect of the deed dated 20-12-80 and on this is essentially a question of fact and relying on the testimony of DW 3 the learned courts below arrived at such a finding and it is a clean finding of fact which cannot be reopened before this Court unless it can be shown that the finding is based on no evidence at all but admittedly there is some evidence for the court to arrive at such finding. So, sufficiency or insufficiency of evidence cannot be the ground for interference by this Court with the impugned judgment and order. The learned Advocate then submits that the main grievance of the pre-emptor petitioner is that both the courts below relying on extraneous evidence arrived at a finding that the deed in question is not a deed of sale, rather it is a deed of release and that contravenes the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act. The learned Advocate further submits that this submission made by Mr. Ruhul Amin, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor, petitioner is not tenable in law inasmuch as section 92 of the Evidence Act prohibits a party to the agreement to lead evidence to add, vary or subtract from the terms of written instrument but in the instant case it is not a question of addition, varying or subtracting which will in the terms of the agreement rather in the instant case the question is what is the nature and character of the deed in question. The pre-emptor petitioner claimed the deed to be a deed of sale whereas the pre-emptee opposite parties claimed that it is a deed of release and in such circumstances the courts were competent to look into the nature and character of the deed in question and perfectly entitled to decide the nature and character of the documents and in support of his contention the learned Advocate relies on the following decisions, namely, 12 DLR 149, 19 DLR 17 and 654, 1988 BLD 33, 1986 BLD 85, AIR 1950 (SC) 15, AIR 1958 (SC) 448 and 1955 (Bombay) 320.
